content: 1. Adenomyosis is characterized by a junctional zone measuring more than 12 mm and the presence of hemorrhagic high-signal myometrial spots, as described by Larsen in 2011. 2. Advances in preoperative diagnostic techniques have facilitated the investigation of new medical and surgical therapies aimed at eliminating the need for hysterectomy. 3. While surgery remains the primary treatment for women who have completed their desired family size, medical therapy is an option for those who wish to preserve fertility and prefer conservative management. 4. Minimally invasive surgical procedures, such as endometrial ablation, resection, laparoscopic excision, and magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound, offer more conservative treatment options. 5. Hormonal therapies for adenomyosis include combined oral contraceptives, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists, danazol, intrauterine devices (IUDs) releasing levonorgestrel or danazol, and aromatase inhibitors. 6. The target tissue for hormonal therapy is the ectopic endometrium. 7. Hormonal therapy is proposed to reduce the proliferation of endometrial cells by acting on the ectopic endometrium, leading to a decrease in uterine volume, reduced menstrual blood loss, and alleviation of dysmenorrhea, as noted by Fedele in 2008. 8. Systemic hormonal therapy suppresses the estrogenic stimulation of the disease by targeting the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, resulting in a hypo-estrogenic state that regresses the lesions. 9. Local hormonal therapy directly targets the ectopic endometrium, inducing atrophy of the endometrial glands and stromal decidualization, as described by Fedele in 1997 and 2008. 10. The rationale for hormonal therapy is to create a localized hypo-estrogenic metabolic state, which induces regression of adenomyosis and alleviates symptoms by reducing abnormal uterine bleeding and pain. 11. Continuous combined oral contraception and high-dose progestins, such as oral norethindrone acetate or subcutaneous depot medroxyprogesterone, have been shown to temporarily induce regression of adenomyosis, as reported by Garcia in 2011. 12. Common side effects of oral contraception and progestins include nausea, breast discomfort, and breakthrough bleeding. 13. GnRH agonists were the first drugs used in the treatment of adenomyosis, as noted by Grow in 1991. 14. GnRH agonists act by binding to GnRH receptors in the pituitary gland, leading to down-regulation of GnRH activity. 15. This mechanism creates a reversible state of medical menopause. 16. GnRH agonist therapy is administered via intramuscular or subcutaneous injection or as a twice-daily nasal spray. 17. This therapy results in a reduction in uterine volume, amenorrhea, and relief of severe dysmenorrhea. 18. However, discontinuation of therapy leads to regrowth of the uterus and recurrence of symptoms, as noted by Grow in 1991. 19. An MRI study by Imaoka in 2002 observed a decrease in the junctional zone width in adenomyosis patients following GnRH-agonist treatment. 20. GnRH agonist therapy may be indicated for women with diffuse adenomyosis seeking pregnancy, as it also promotes uterine and endometrial receptivity. 21. This therapy is typically used for limited periods of three to six months due to adverse effects, including hot flashes and decreased bone mineral density. 22. GnRH agonists may control adenomyosis symptoms during therapy, but their use is limited due to side effects and the potential rebound effect after cessation of treatment. 23. GnRH agonists are often reserved for cases where immediate conception is desired or as preoperative treatment to facilitate surgery by reducing uterine volume and vascularization, as described by Lin in 2000. 24. The insertion of a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device (IUD) leads to endometrial gland atrophy and extensive decidual transformation of the stroma. 25. Levonorgestrel-releasing IUDs have been found to down-regulate estrogen receptors in the endometrium. 26. Danazol-loaded intrauterine devices induce remission of dysmenorrhea, reduce menstrual bleeding, and allow spontaneous conception after removal of the IUD, as noted by Fedele in 1997 and 2008. 27. The rationale for treating adenomyosis with aromatase inhibitors lies in their ability to inhibit the enzyme aromatase P450, which is expressed in the ectopic endometrium, as described by Fedele in 1997 and Kitawaki in 2006. 28. Common side effects of aromatase inhibitors include joint and muscle pain. 29. Additionally, aromatase inhibitors are associated with loss of bone density, leading to higher rates of osteoporosis and bone fractures, as well as hot flashes, as reported by Crew in 2007. 30. Hysterectomy has traditionally been the most common treatment for symptomatic adenomyosis. 31. However, hysterectomy is associated with perioperative and postoperative morbidity, decreased quality of life, and high healthcare costs. 32. It is estimated that hysterectomies account for the majority of these costs, which were recently estimated to exceed USD 2.1 billion annually in the United States, as noted by Cardozo in 2012. 33. Hysterectomy is not appropriate for women who wish to preserve their fertility. 34. The availability of noninvasive imaging techniques has enabled the preoperative diagnosis of adenomyosis. 35. A noninvasive approach to adenomyosis management is increasingly being explored to reduce the need for hysterectomy.
